item.title: Best laptops for engineering students: Top 4 picks for power and portability
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 1.34
Engineering students are constantly on the move. Lectures, labs, libraries. That’s why you need a laptop that can handle your workload without making you feel like you’re lugging around a block of concrete. That’s why the laptops below strike such a good balance. They’re powerful for CAD and simulations, but they’re also light enough to throw in a bag and carry around campus. Why you should trust PCWorld for laptop reviews and buying advice: It’s in our name! PCWorld prides itself on laptop experience and expertise. We’ve been covering PCs since 1983, and we now review more than 70 laptops every year. All of the picks below have been personally tested and vetted by our experts, who’ve applied not only performance benchmarks but rigorous usability standards. We’re also committed to reviewing PC laptops at every price point to help you find a machine that matches your budget. Asus Zenbook 14 OLED – Best overall Pros Robust build quality Attractive OLED touchscreen Good CPU and integrated GPU performance Outstanding battery life Cons Design is dull Keyboard isn’t memorable Mediocre connectivity Price When Reviewed: $849.99 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price 10% off original price $759 View Deal Asus $999.99 View Deal $1,359 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide Who should buy the Asus Zenbook 14 OLED? The Asus Zenbook 14 OLED tops our list because of the brilliant combination of power, portability, and battery life. The AMD Ryzen 7 chip is designed to run heavier programs like CAD without slowing down, even if you’ve got a bunch of tabs open on the side. The 14-inch 1920×1200 OLED touchscreen also looks fantastic and will make your diagrams and other projects really pop. The one thing that really sticks out is the battery, though. Seriously, it went for over 16 hours in our test, which kind of blew my mind. You can definitely survive a whole day of classes, especially with conservative use and the brightness turned down. The audio is also quite good, offering you good volume and clarity during remote lectures. Asus Zenbook 14 OLED: Further considerations The build quality’s pretty good, especially considering it’s just $699 as of this writing. It’s also thin (0.59 inches) and light (2.82 pounds), which is great if you’re running from class to class. While the keyboard isn’t the best we’ve ever used because of the undersized keys, it’s totally fine for day-to-day use. Read our full Asus Zenbook 14 OLED review Dell 14S – Best battery life Pros Class-leading battery life Slick build Colorful and accurate display Good port selection Cons Dismal 3D performance Display isn’t very bright So-so performance for the money Price When Reviewed: $1,469 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price 8% off original price $1349.99 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide Who should buy the Dell 14S? The Dell 14S is a great fit for engineering students who want a laptop that can easily last through a long day of classes. It actually delivered some of the longest runtimes we’ve seen (nearly 36 hours in our video playback test!), thanks in part to its efficient Intel Core Ultra 7 355 processor and 69 watt-hour battery. It’s also just a solid day-to-day machine. The aluminum design feels nice and sturdy, the keyboard is comfortable to type on for long periods of time, and the laptop remains easy to carry at just 3.28 pounds. For students who mainly use office apps, the Dell 14S has more than enough power for that kind of thing. Dell 14S: Further considerations This isn’t the laptop to buy if you need raw performance. The Dell 14S relies on Intel integrated graphics rather than a dedicated GPU, so it’s not the best choice for running demanding CAD projects. Ultimately, the Dell 14S is a portable, reliable machine for students who spend most of their day away from a desk. It puts efficiency first. Acer Nitro V 16 AI – Best for work and gaming on a budget Pros Large touchpad compared to alternatives 16-inch 1200p display at a low price Lots of physical connectivity Good battery life for a budget gaming laptop Cons Sub-par CPU performance Terrible audio quality from built-in speakers Wireless connectivity stuck on the Wi-Fi 6 standards Slightly more expensive laptops offer better value Price When Reviewed: $899 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price 7% off original price $828.98 View Deal $1168.99 View Deal $1,269 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide Who should buy the Acer Nitro V 16 AI? If you’re an engineering student who likes to game after class, the Acer Nitro V 16 AI is worth considering. The RTX 5050 tucked inside delivers smooth 1080p gaming, hitting a respectable 72 FPS in Cyberpunk 2077 on Ultra settings. It also gives extra firepower for CAD modeling and rendering tasks. The 16-inch 1920×1200 IPS display is slightly taller than the typical 15.6-inch 1080p screens, so you’re getting more vertical workspace here–this is useful for coding, spreadsheets, and so on. At a price hovering between $800 and $900 it’s a budget-friendly option for students. Acer Nitro V 16 AI: Further considerations The AMD Ryzen 5 240 isn’t the fastest CPU around, and the speakers aren’t impressive, but despite these trade-offs, the Acer Nitro V 16 AI avoids common pitfalls most budget gaming laptops fall into. It lasted 12 hours on a single charge in testing, which is impressive for a gaming machine. The keyboard and touchpad are also spacious, making it comfortable to work on for long periods. Read our full Acer Nitro V 16 AI review Microsoft Surface Pro – Best ultraportable Pros Compact and well-built Good office performance All Copilot Plus features available Good battery life Cons Narrow screen to work on No HDR support No charger included Price When Reviewed: $799.99 Best Prices Today: Retailer Price 8% off original price $729.99 View Deal $949.99 View Deal $1039.99 View Deal $1049 View Deal $1149.99 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide View more prices Who should buy the Microsoft Surface Pro? If you’re an engineering student with a jam-packed schedule, often needing to run from class to class, the Surface Pro is so lightweight (just a little over a pound) you’ll hardly notice its presence. Inside this laptop you’ll find a Snapdragon X Plus chip, so you can expect it to deliver a quiet, fanless experience (perfect for working in libraries and lecture halls), and it should handle basic coding and homework just fine. Note: Snapdragon X Plus / Arm models are fine for lighter coding and notes, but if your coursework is heavy on SolidWorks, Autodesk apps, or older MATLAB workflows an x86 Windows laptop is a safer bet for performance and app compatibility first. The 12-inch 2196×1464 screen offers sharp colors and touchscreen capabilities, allowing you to draw and take notes with the (optical) Slim Pen. Microsoft Surface Pro: Further considerations Though we really vibe with the high-resolution display, it’s a bit small if you’re the kind of person that has many windows open at once. Battery life is all over the place, ranging from two to three hours under heavy loads to 19 hours with light usage. You’re also limited to just two USB-C ports, so you’ll probably want to pick up a dock or hub. Read our full Microsoft Surface Pro 2025 review Other notable laptops we’ve tested Geekom GeekBook M16 : The GeekBook M16 is a solid budget productivity laptop with outstanding battery life and build quality, but its weak display and limited graphics performance hold it back from being a true all-rounder. Dell XPS 13 : Dell’s XPS 13 is a compelling budget laptop, even if it falls just slightly behind the MacBook Neo. Asus Zenbook A16 : A solid productivity laptop, with top-notch office performance, an outstanding multimedia experience, and excellent battery life MSI Prestige 16 Flip AI+ : The MSI Prestige 16 Flip AI+ is a great laptop with a quality build, zippy speeds in everyday operation, and a wonderful display for work and play. How we test laptops The PCWorld team puts each and every Windows laptop through a series of benchmarks that test GPU and CPU performance, battery life, and so on. The idea is to push the laptop to its limits and then compare it against others we’ve tested. Chromebooks, on the other hand, go through a series of web-based tests. For a much deeper look at our review methodology, check out how PCWorld tests laptops . Who curated this article? Hi, I’m Ashley Biancuzzo , and I oversee all laptop and Chromebook coverage at PCWorld. While you’ll see me review Chromebooks on occasion, I’m also really into the broader world of consumer tech. I spend a lot of time writing and thinking about where laptops are headed–from AI and sustainable designs to long-term trends. When I’m not deep in the world of tech, you’ll probably find me gaming, getting lost in a good book, or chilling with my rescue greyhound, Allen. How to choose the best laptop for engineering students The following are important questions to ask before making a purchase. How much power do you need? You’ll need a good amount of power. Engineering classes usually have you running some pretty heavy stuff like CAD, MATLAB, SolidWorks, and simulations. That stuff can slow your laptop down if it’s not up to the task, especially if you’ve got a bunch of apps open. A Core i5 or Ryzen 5 will get you through most of it, but if you want things to run smoother, a Core i7 or Ryzen 7 is where it’s at (so long as your wallet agrees). Is RAM important? For sure! You’ll be using code editors, compilers, simulation tools, sometimes all at once. RAM keeps your laptop from freezing up when you’ve got a ton going on. And with RAM prices being a bit volatile nowadays, it’s worth future-proofing if you can. 8GB might work if you’re just starting out, but 16GB is way better, especially later on when your classes get more intense. How much storage should you get? You’ll collect a ton of files–project folders, software installs, maybe some video editing or game dev work depending on your focus. We’d say go for at least 512GB SSD so you’re not constantly clearing space. If you can get 1TB, do it. It’s faster and gives you more breathing room for whatever your classes (or side hobbies) throw at you. FAQ 1. What is the best laptop for engineering students? If you’re an engineering student who needs something light, fast, and reliable for coding or writing papers (plus a great screen and battery), the Asus Zenbook 14 OLED is a dang fine pick. 2. What is the best budget laptop for engineering students? If you’re on a tight budget and just need a straightforward for lighter coding programs, the Acer Aspire Go 15 gets the job done for just under $500. 3. Is battery life important for engineering students? Heck yeah! Long battery life means you can power through those long nights at the school library. 4. What’s the ideal screen size for an engineering laptop? We’d say the best screen size is anywhere from 13- to 15-inches. It can’t be too cumbersome otherwise it’ll get difficult to carry around. item.title: Windows’ September update breaks File History. The fix is a rollback
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 1.14
Many users who have installed the latest September security patches for Windows have found that the “File History” feature no longer works—deleted or corrupted files can no longer be recovered. File History automatically saves copies of files, allowing users to recover accidentally deleted or corrupted files using older versions that were stored hours, days, or weeks ago. By default, File History backs up all folders in the user profile (Documents, Music, Pictures, Videos, and Desktop) to an external drive, such as a USB flash drive or a network attached storage (NAS) device. According to Microsoft, the issue is due to a bug that occurs in all current versions of Windows 10 and 11, including 21H2, 22H2, 23H2, 24H2, 25H2, and 26H1. Microsoft wrote on this support page and this one : After installing the September 2026 Windows security update, some customers using File History, might be unable to create or update backups. File History, available through Control Panel > System and Security > File History, is used to back up files to an external drive or network location. Affected devices might incorrectly display a “Reconnect your drive” message even when a compatible backup drive is connected and functioning properly. Additionally, the “Last Backup” timestamp might not update, and previously backed up files might show “No previous version available.” In some cases, Event Viewer might record application crash events referencing FileHistory.exe and KERNELBASE.dll . There’s currently no fix for the issue, though Microsoft says it is “working on a resolution” that’ll come in a future Windows update. Until an official fix is released, the best solution is to uninstall the security update, which you can do by rolling back a problematic Windows update .

item.title: Microsoft Defender is causing slow VLC startups. Here’s the fix
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 1.04
For some time now, there have been complaints across various online forums about how the popular VLC Media Player takes several seconds (sometimes half a minute!) to start up. The problem occurs regardless of size or the type of media file you wish to play. There’s also some unfounded accusations against the VideoLan developers; one often reads claims that Microsoft is deliberately slowing down the open-source media player. However, this theory is contradicted by the fact that this problem only affects some Windows computers. For instance, on one of my PCs running Windows 10, this “moment of silence” when launching VLC has been noticeable for some time. But on a Windows 11 PC, the problem doesn’t occur. Reports from affected users on Reddit suggest the question of whether the issue lies with Windows 10 or 11 misses the crux of the problem. There must be another cause. One thing the affected computers seem to have in common is that Microsoft Defender, which protects against malware, is active. There are no known reports of similar issues with other antivirus software. The VideoLan developers, led by Jean-Baptiste Kempf, have also accused Microsoft on X/Twitter of being responsible for the slowdown. There has not yet been an official response from Microsoft. This is because of a « bug » from Microsoft Defender in one update of Windows 11, who magically made VLC plugins cache quarantined by Windows. Reinstalling VLC or regeneration of the plugin cache will fix this. Calling open source software embarrassing when it is a Windows… https://t.co/IFLrXFZFsv — VideoLAN (@videolan) August 12, 2026 Investigations have revealed that, following an update a few weeks ago, Microsoft Defender has been placing the VLC Player’s plug-in cache (plugins.dat) in quarantine, which causes the program to boot slowly. A faulty Defender signature update (version 1.455.50.0) and the Windows Update KB5121003 are said to be responsible. Microsoft released the latter as part of its patch on August 11th and it has caused a host of problems ever since. However, the VLC Media Player’s start-up issue has, in some cases, been around for quite a while. Workaround for VLC Media Player To make VLC Media Player start normally again (usually within a second), reset the plug-in cache. You don’t even have to edit the registry or delete files manually. Instead, you can either reinstall VLC Media Player or instruct the program itself to regenerate the cache. To do this, use vlc-cache-gen.exe . Click on the search icon (magnifying glass) in the bottom left-hand corner and type VLC in the search box. The top result should be VLC media player – reset preferences and cache files . Click on this and run it–this will reset the settings and cache. fz By the way, since Microsoft hasn’t released a fix for Defender yet, the problem might reoccur. To prevent this, set an exclusion in Defender for VLC Media Player. This basically tells Defender not to scan the directory for malware. This does involve a certain risk, especially if you didn’t download the VLC Media Player from the manufacturer’s website. To set the exclusion in Microsoft Defender, go to the following in Windows 10: Settings Windows Security Virus & Threat Protection Virus & Threat Protection Settings > Manage Settings Exclusions Add or remove exclusions {User Account Control security prompt} ≫ Add exclusion ≫ Folder >> Select the folder C:\Program Files\VideoLAN\VLC\plugins . In Windows 11, the procedure is similar: Settings Privacy and Security Windows Security > Then continue as described above

item.title: Mac Studio (M5 Max) review: Shifting into overdrive
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
At a glance Expert's Rating Pros Dramatic SSD speed boost Enhanced external display support Cons RAM and SSD are not user upgradeable Our Verdict The Mac Studio’s SSD speed improvement is so dramatic that even if you bought an M4 Max or M3 Ultra Mac Studio–the previous models–you should consider upgrading to the M5 Max Mac Studio. Plus, the external display support is expanded. Sure it’s expensive, but if you want the best Mac ever made, accept no substitute. Price When Reviewed This value will show the geolocated pricing text for product undefined Best Pricing Today Price When Reviewed $2,499 Best Prices Today: Apple Mac Studio (M5 Max, 2026) Retailer Price $2,449.99 View Deal $2499 View Deal Price comparison from over 24,000 stores worldwide With the M5 Max Mac Studio, there’s good news, and there’s great news. The good news is that it offers faster CPU processing and graphics. It’s a marginal boost over the previous generation, but faster is always good. The great news is that the improved SSD speed that was introduced with the M5 MacBook Pro comes to Apple’s top Mac. The faster SSD is such a big deal that if you’re in a production environment and you invested in an M4 Max or M3 Ultra Mac Studio, you should seriously consider upgrading, even if the prices are higher. Time is money, and an investment in the current Mac Studio will be money well spent. Here’s our in-depth review of the M5 Max Mac Studio . Editor’s note: This review originally published on Macworld.com . M5 Max Mac Studio: Our model’s specifications The Mac Studio is available in two standard configurations: A $2,499 model with an M5 Max chip (18-core CPU, 32-core GPU) and 36GB of RAM, and a $5,499 model with an M5 Ultra chip with 96GB of RAM. Customers can customize their purchase by adjusting the number of CPU and GPU cores, and add more memory and SSD storage. This review focuses on the M5 Max Mac Studio with a chip upgrade, additional RAM, and a larger SSD. Here are the specs of our review unit: CPU : M5 Max with 18 cores (6 super cores, 12 performance cores), 16-core Neural Engine GPU : 40 cores Memory : 128GB unified memory (614GBps memory bandwidth) Storage : 4TB SSD Ports : 4 Thunderbolt 5/USB-C; 10Gb ethernet; 2 USB-A (USB 3); HDMI 2.1; 3.5mm audio; 2 USB-C; SDXC Card slot Networking : Wi‑Fi 7 (802.11be); Bluetooth 6; Threads; 10Gb ethernet Weight : 6 pounds (2.7 kg) Dimensions : 3.7 x 7.7 x 7.7 inches (9.5 x 19.7 x 19.7 cm) Price (as tested) : $6,899/£6,899/CA$10,099/AU$10,899 The Mac Studio design reamins unchanged from its introduction in 2022. Fundry M5 Max Mac Studio: Performance The odd M4 Max and M3 Ultra offerings Apple had with the previous Mac Studio were due to Apple skipping a generation with its Ultra chips . This time around, Apple decided that the M5 series would have an Ultra chip, so you can get either an M5 Max or M5 Ultra. The $2,499 M5 Max Mac Studio comes standard with an 18-core CPU (6 super cores, 12 performance cores), a 32-core GPU, 36GB of unified memory, and a 512GB SSD. However, this CPU is essentially fixed at 36GB of RAM; if you want more, you must upgrade to the 18-core CPU/40-core GPU, which technically costs $300 but actually adds $600 to the price when the cost of the 48GB RAM upgrade is factored in. It can further be upgraded to 64GB ($400) or 128GB ($2,000). This review looks at the M5 Max option with an 18-core CPU, a 40-core GPU, 128GB of RAM, and a 4TB SSD, which adds $4,400 the price of the Mac Studio. More about the pricing at the end of this review. Blackmagic Disk Tests Foundry Typically, we start our reviews by looking at overall performance with Geekbench, and then we work our way through more specific aspects. But the SSD performance is so overwhelmingly good, it’s the story here. I mean, this chart doesn’t look correct, does it? Apple improved SSD performance with the M5 chip series, and we’ve seen big improvements in the M5 MacBook Pro. It’s finally come to the Mac Studio–it’s almost a shame that we had to wait so long. This is one of the key reasons why you should upgrade from another Mac Studio, even if you bought one this year. It’s a difference you’ll definitely feel. Geekbench 7 Results are expressed as Geekbench scores. Higher scores/longer bars are faster. Foundry Geekbench 7 was released just this year; it’s a general-purpose benchmark tool for gauging performance. The previous-generation M3 Ultra is faster than the M5 Max in multi-core CPU testing, but only by 9 percent. The difference between the M5 Max and the M4 Max that it replaces is more substantial at 22 percent. The M5 Max’s Single-core CPU results are 8 percent faster than those of the M4 Max. We’ve seen improvements of 8 to 10 percent from generation to generation, so that result remains consistent. Geekbench 6 Results are expressed as Geekbench scores. Higher scores/longer bars are faster. Foundry Since Geekbench 7 is pretty new, we tested with Geekbench 6 for reference. Here, the M5 Max beats the M3 Ultra, but the margin is only 7 percent in the Multi-core tests–a difference you may not notice. Cinebench 2026 Results are expressed as Cinebench scores. Higher scores/longer bars are faster. Foundry Maxon also has a benchmark tool that tests more strenuously than Geekbench. Unfortunately, we don’t have data from older Mac Studios, so the results here are presented with the M5 Pro Mac mini and the M5 MacBook Pro. Still, you can get a sense of how much and improvement you can experience if you move up the chip series. Cinebench 2024 Results are expressed as Cinebench scores. Higher scores/longer bars are faster. Foundry We do have Cinebench 2024 results from the previous Mac Studio lineup, and the M5 Max provides a 10 percent GPU boost over the M3 Ultra. The GPU improvement over the M4 Max is a more noticeable 33 percent. Geekbench AI Neural Engine Results are expressed as Geekbench scores. Higher scores/longer bars are faster. Foundry Geekbench AI GPU Results are expressed as Geekbench scores. Higher scores/longer bars are faster. Foundry The Mac Studio has become extremely popular for AI development. Our benchmark records don’t go that far back with this test, so we’ve included other M5 chips for reference. The M5 Max’s Neural Engine offers a vast improvement over the M4 Max and the M3 Ultra–that a boon for AI developers. One thing to consider with the Mac Studio and AI is the RAM configuration. To get more than 36GB of RAM, you need to upgrade from the base M4 Max chip, which bumps the price by at least $600, as I outlined earlier. iMovie video export Results are times in seconds. Lower times/shorter bars are faster. Foundry The speed gain that the M4 Max had over the M2 Max Mac Studio was much more significant than the one we see between the M4 Max and M5 Max. Keep in mind that the previous comparison actually skips a chip generation since Apple didn’t make an M3 Max Mac Studio. Handbrake video encode Results are times in seconds. Lower times/shorter bars are faster. Foundry Another test where the difference between the M4/M5 Max and M2 Max are drastic. The change is much more dramatic when you do not use hardware acceleration. Geekbench 7 Compute Results are expressed as Geekbench scores. Higher scores/longer bars are faster. Foundry The M3 Ultra posts faster Metal scores in Geekbench 7’s Compute test, but it has a CPU with twice as many core (80 versus the M5 Max’s 40-cores). Geekbench 6 Compute Results are expressed as Geekbench scores. Higher scores/longer bars are faster. Foundry With Geekbench 6, the M3 Ultra shows a more significant lead over the M5 Max, but again, it’s an 80-core GPU against a 40-core CPU. Video game benchmarks Results are frames per second. Higher rates/longer bars are faster. Foundry We saw frame rate boosts of 30 percent or more in Total War: Warhammer III and Borderlands 3 . Our results with Civilization VI , an older game, were flat. In all, the multi-core CPU improvements are a tad bit more than the typical increase of 15 percent (or so) that we’ve seen between generations, with the M5 Max showing a boost of 20 percent or more over the M4 Max in many of our tests. If the CPU performance isn’t enough to convince you to upgrade, then take a look at the GPU, where the M5 Max even outperforms the M3 Ultra. Combine that with the SSD improvement, and what we have is proof that Apple can continue to offer significant progress with its chips to make the cheaper Mac Studio a compelling machine atop the Mac lineup. M5 Max Mac Studio: Thunderbolt 5 ports Apple upgraded the Thunderbolt ports to Thunderbolt 5 with the previous Mac Studio, so those same ports are on the current model. The throughput is 80Gbps that can go up as high as 120Gbps, but you need a Thunderbolt 5 cable and a supported device to reach those top speeds. Mac Studio rear ports. Fundry The M5 Max Mac Studio supports up to five displays, four over Thunderbolt at 6K/60Hz or 4K/165Hz, and one connected to the HDMI port at 5K/60Hz. The M5 Max Mac Studio also can drive three displays, with two displays at 8K/60Hz or 5K/120Hz or 4K/240Hz, and a third HDMI display at 5K/60Hz. These supported specs are improved over the M4 Max Mac Studio, so the new Mac Studio’s display support gets a boost. M5 Max Mac Studio: Same ol’ good stuff This iteration of the Mac Studio is a chip upgrade and nothing much else (besides the boosted display support, which is tied to the chip.) The design is the same as it has been since the Mac Studio’s introduction in 2022, and it’s not likely to change for a long while. The port configuration is also the same, and the keyboard, mouse, and display are sold separately. Speaking of display, Apple did release new displays earlier this year, though you might be able to find something comparable to Apple’s $1,499 Studio Display –it’s not a bad display, it’s just that it’s quite pricey. The Studio Display XDR is also expensive, but it’s the display that professionals who demand top-notch color and image quality will want. M5 Max Mac Studio: Price Except for its non-upgradeable design, there hasn’t been a “catch” with the Mac Studio until now. That catch is the higher price. The base M5 Max model starts at $2,499, a $500 increase over the M4 Max Mac Studio, but no more expensive that it was after Apple hiked prices in June. However, the Ultra Mac Studio went up in price again. In June, Apple increased the M3 Ultra Mac Studio’s starting price from $3,999 to $5,299, and now Apple has raised the starting price of the M5 Ultra another $200 to $5,499. Apple increased the Mac Studio price last June, and made more price increases with this new release. Foundry These are steep increases, enough to make anyone pause, even if you’re using a model from the M2 generation. If you feel like you can’t ever get enough speed, then you won’t blink at the higher prices. Others might want to wait. But I think these higher prices aren’t going to go down, even if the supply chain shortages that cause them eventually get resolved. These prices are the new normal , so some Mac buyers will need to reset their personal upgrade cycles. Should you buy the M5 Max Mac Studio? If you’re a Mac Studio user, you need a fast Mac. Apple’s improvements to the SSD are so compelling that even if you have an M4 Max or M3 Ultra Mac Studio, you should consider upgrading. Yes, it’s a pricey proposition, but your workflow will notice the improvement. But if you have a older Mac Studio and working with AI, you could wait for the next generation, because future M-series chips promise to have better AI capabilities. In that case, waiting isn’t a bad idea. However, like I said, the Mac Studio is a pricey proposition, and if you’re an individual professional whose means of offsetting the cost of purchase aren’t as immediate as, say, someone in a bigger production house, then continue to enjoy your current Mac Studio investment. It’s the official launch day for Google’s refreshed take on laptops. You can read my impressions here — long story short, it seems to be a platform made with phone-first users in mind. But if you’ve decided that you’re interested and want to pick one up, you have a choice of five at the launch, from the biggest names in the laptop industry: Acer, Asus, Dell, HP, and Lenovo. Pre-orders open today, both at Google’s official online store (at least in the US) and various retailers, with deliveries planned for October 4th. Google has set a few minimum standards for Googlebooks, notably 16GB of RAM (far more than the cheapest Chromebooks), an Intel or Qualcomm processor (MediaTek models are planned later), and a touchscreen. Acer Googlebook 14 — $899 Michael Crider/Foundry CPU: Intel Core Ultra 5 series 3 325 RAM: 16 GB Storage: 512GB Screen: 14″ 2880×1800 OLED touchscreen, 120Hz Trackpad: Gorilla Glass Weight: 2.51 pounds (1.13 kg) Ports: USB-C x 3 Acer has the cheapest laptop in this initial blitz. It’s also the most typical, just barely making it out of the area of “budget” laptops compared to Windows models, thanks to its luscious OLED touchscreen with boosted resolution and refresh rate. It’s on the light side with no obvious exotic materials in its construction, and lacks some extras like a haptic trackpad. Strangely, it’s the only fully convertible (Yoga-style) laptop among the first batch. Asus Googlebook 14 — $1299 Michael Crider/Foundry CPU: Intel Core Ultra 5 series 3 325 RAM: 16 GB Storage: 512GB Screen: 14″ 2880×1800 OLED touchscreen, 120Hz Weight: 2.18 pounds (.98 kg) Ports: USB-C x 2, USB-A, HDMI With a whopping $400 price jump over the nearly identically named Acer model, you can really see the range of the initial models. The Asus design is slimmer and sleeker with an all-metal shell and a pleasingly rough texture, very similar to the Zenbook A14. Even though it’s using an Intel processor and packs six speakers, it’s claimed to last 16 hours thanks to a boosted 70-watt hour battery. I also like the broader port selection. Dell XPS Googlebook — $1199 Michael Crider/Foundry CPU: Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite RAM: 16 GB Storage: 512GB Screen: 13.4″ 2560×1600 IPS touchscreen, 120Hz Weight: 2.2 pounds (.99 kg) Ports: USB-C x 2 If there’s one device that surprised me at Google’s press event, it’s this one. This is, indeed, a Dell XPS model, sleek and light as that implies. If I hadn’t known the context I would have assumed it was a standard XPS 13. With the smaller screen and Snapdragon processor, and 18 hours of quoted battery life, this is the road warrior of the bunch. Interestingly, Best Buy is showing a lower price than Google, “just” $999 . HP Googlebook 14 — $1299 Michael Crider/Foundry CPU: Qualcomm Snapdragon X Elite RAM: 16 GB Storage: 512GB Screen: 14″ 2880×1800 OLED touchscreen, 120Hz Weight: 2.74 pounds (.98 kg) Ports: USB-C x 2 HP’s initial Googlebook offering feels a lot like the Asus model, though not quite as sleek…which is strange, since it’s using a Snapdragon processor. And I have to say that it’s lower-rated battery life (15 hours) and considerably heavier weight for the same screen size (2.74 pounds) really don’t look great in comparison, for all that these laptops appear similar. The only standout on the spec list is a fingerprint reader integrated into the power button. Lenovo Googlebook 15 — $1099 Michael Crider/Foundry CPU: Intel Core Ultra 5 series 3 325 RAM: 16 GB Storage: 512GB Screen: 15.3″ 2880×1800 OLED touchscreen, 120Hz Trackpad: Gorilla Glass Weight: 2.68 pounds (1.22 kg) Ports: USB-C x 2, USB-A, HDMI The only initial laptop in this range that stretches into the mid-size category comes from Lenovo. Though its screen is 15.3 inches, it’s using a similar OLED panel and 2.8K resolution as several others, and I liked the wavy texture of the bottom, very reminiscent of the Pixelbook Go. You also get a fingerprint reader and some big speakers flanking the keyboard, and Lenovo’s typical manual privacy shutter on the webcam. But a bigger screen without a bigger battery means less longevity. I hesitate to offer a standout pick after only a couple of hours to compare these laptops, but the Acer model with its convertible screen and low price and the Dell XPS with its super-sleek chassis made the biggest impressions on me. Reviews will be coming later, and as I recommended in my editorial , I would hesitate against pre-orders until those reviews come out. More models are already in the pipeline, including at least one Lenovo tablet that’s been spotted already . Oh, and one last warning, which was reiterated to me more than once during the Google preview event: With the RAM and storage issues plaguing the market, don’t be surprised to see those prices go up sooner rather than later.

item.title: The Googlebook’s most compelling AI feature isn’t even AI
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Google’s new Googlebooks are finally here! As promised, they come with a bevy of flashy Gemini features, including an AI-enabled mouse pointer, a local dictation tool, and the ability to create desktop widgets with prompts. But the Googlebook AI feature that really got my attention isn’t, strictly speaking, an AI feature. First, let’s talk about the Gemini-infused “ Magic Pointer ,” which lets you select or lasso text, images, and other elements. From there it gets sent off to Gemini for further explanation, rewrites, or other AI duties. Among the major Gemini features for Google’s new class of $899-and-up Googlebooks, now available for pre-order from the likes of Acer, Asus, Dell, and Lenovo, the Magic Pointer can be summoned with a wiggle of the mouse. It makes its presence known with a little “+” next to the pointer. The Magic Pointer lets you select text, lasso images, and interact with other desktop elements, which you can then send to Gemini as context. Ben Patterson/Foundry I got the chance to play around with the Magic Pointer during a Google pre-briefing last week. Select a block of text and the Magic Pointer will send it to Gemini for further analysis or tweaking. You can also circle an image and ask Gemini, “What is this?” The bot will then explain what “this” is. There’s also another Gemini-powered feature called Rambler. It’s imported from Gboard and it’s designed to organize your ramblings thoughts into smooth, flowing text. You can paste transcribed text from the Rambler anywhere you like, including into a Gmail message. You can also deploy it via the Quick Insert tool, which you can summon using a dedicated Googlebook key. Just tap the Quick Insert key (the one with the little “+” above the Shift key) to summon the Rambler. Ben Patterson/Foundry Another Gemini feature for Googlebooks is the ability to create desktop widgets using natural-language prompts. This means you can ask Gemini to build a desktop widget that displays information from your family’s upcoming information like the flight information and hotel reservation. All of those details are plucked from Gmail or other connected Google sources. These various Gemini tricks (which can be individually enabled or deactivated from Googlebook’s system settings) work using a combination of local and cloud AI models. Local AI generally handles lower-level duties such as basic transcription and text selection, while cloud AI tackles anything more involved, including chats, text editing, online research, and other complex AI chores. (Cloud-based Gemini features must be managed from your Google account settings.) Indeed, the most powerful Gemini functionality on Googlebooks is already available to anyone with access to a Chrome browser. That includes Antigravity, the Google vibe-coding tool that comes loaded on Googlebooks, but uses cloud-based Gemini and Claude models just as it does on Windows or Mac devices. That said, here comes the Googlebooks AI feature I’m more bullish on and, as I noted earlier, it’s not actually AI. Instead, we’re talking native support for fully isolated Linux environments, which Antigravity users can easily spin up or tear down via an Explorer-like interface. Google Antigravity users will get the most out of the Googlebook’s native support for Linux virtual machines. Ben Patterson/Foundry The Linux virtual machines on Chromebooks are siloed by a Level 5 security-certified hypervisor powered by pKVM isolation (a first for laptops, Google says), while the Googlebook’s main internals and OS are walled off by Google Titan security, “defense in-depth” architecture, and on-device malware protection. In everyday terms, that means Antigravity users can quickly spawn secure, fully isolated Linux playgrounds for their Googlebook vibe-coding projects, while keeping their laptop’s core system architecture safe from those virtual Linux machines and the coding agents inside them. Of course, Linux virtual machines won’t be anything new to seasoned developers, and they’re readily available for Windows and Mac systems. That said, installing and configuring Linux VMs can be tricky unless you know what you’re doing. On a Googlebook, all the heavy lifting has already been done for you. Now… is a Googlebook’s native support for Linux virtual machines reason enough to buy one? Probably not. If anything, the Googlebook’s tight integration with other Android devices is a far more compelling reason. ( My colleague Michael Crider has that angle covered. ) And, to be perfectly clear, no one should make the mistake of confusing a Googlebook with a (hypothetical) Geminibook. The Googlebook boasts its own native Gemini features, yes, but it’s not an offline Gemini replacement. But if you asked me for a Googlebook’s most compelling and native AI feature, I’d point to the Linux virtual machine support — which, I know, isn’t really AI.

item.title: Why the dumbest headphones might be the smartest ones
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
I take it back. I was wrong to scoff at the kids. A few months ago, an article crossed my feeds about wired earbuds. According to my juniors, this retro tech represents elegancy and simplicity—a better time. I was initially appalled at the characterization. Having lived through tangled wires and multiple snapped cords, I know exactly how Bluetooth headphone dominance came about. But after yet another confirmation of a security vulnerability in a wireless audio device, I’ve been rethinking my position. Welcome to Safe Mode, your weekly report for pressing security and privacy news—and what steps to take next. Want this newsletter to come directly to your inbox? Sign up on our website ! This particular situation involves Skullcandy’s Dime 3 earbuds. According to Carnegie Mellon University’s cybersecurity response team (CERT), these wireless earbuds will accept pairing requests without user verification . Any nearby, unpaired devices can link with the Dime 3 to record audio input from the microphones, take over audio playback, change the earbuds’ audio profile, or disrupt the user’s connection. If attacked, those who own Skullcandy Dime 3 buds may hear an audio alert of a new device being paired, but may not recognize the significance of the notification. Skullcandy is not unique in being vulnerable to this kind of flaw—this news follows on the heels of Apple’s Beats Studio Buds and Creative’s Sound Blaster Katana V2X soundbar also falling prey to audio hijacking over Bluetooth. But Skullcandy Dime 3 owners may not have access to a fix. If your pair has older firmware, it remains exploitable. Skullcandy has yet to enable a way to update the buds’ internal software, so that the security patch is applied. I’m likely not in imminent danger of being hacked through Bluetooth headphones, but I’m mindful of how connected devices can serve as entryways to juicier information. I don’t want someone to listen in my calls, for example. The easiest solution is to switch to tech that can’t be as easily hacked. Going old-school currently seems the smarter way to go from a cybersecurity standpoint, and in this case, that’s choosing wired devices over wireless. (I’m reminded, as a nerd of a certain vintage, of the phone system in Battlestar Galactica .) Before, taking this stance would have painted me as an antiquarian (or even a Luddite). But the kids, in their wisdom, have instead made it a smart trend. They really are going to be all right. In the news The world is becoming less and less private—and in some ways, less safe by extension. Flock cameras were discovered to take extensive photos of passing cars, OpenAI lets other people see more of your chat prompts than you might think, and Anthropic wants to analyze your financial habits. Each situation sounds innocuous on the surface, but the data shared can reveal much more of your life than you’d want. Swello / Unsplash The concerning: Ever wonder what lives on a Flock camera ? Hackers did and ended up finding roughly 1.6 million images of cars, taken over a three-week period. The cam also had software capable of detecting people, though no facial recognition took place on the camera. (However, this discovery does not prevent such actions happening after photos upload to a central server.) Other people may be reading your ChatGPT prompts , according to 404 Media. Called “Project Lily,” the initiative has humans evaluate the chatbot’s responses to prompts. As a result, any sensitive information related to your health, finances, and more could be seen by strangers. Be cautious about what you share. Anthropic now supports direct links to bank accounts from within Claude. Called “ Claude Money ,” it is the latest company to offer financial analysis as an AI chatbot feature. (OpenAI also allows you to link financial accounts to ChatGPT.) Given that chatbot transcripts may not be as private as one would hope (see above), I advise caution in embracing this feature. The bad: Hackers keep putting old attack methods to work. This time, malicious JavaScript is back , installing browser extensions in Chrome and Edge without user approval. If infected, users can leak credentials, fall victim to meddler-in-the-middle attacks, have their activity screenshotted, and more. To protect yourself, don’t manually open JavaScript files. Tip of the week Alaina Yee / Foundry Speaking of low tech solutions to high tech problems—are you worried about someone spying on you through your webcam? You can get back some peace of mind by literally covering the camera on your devices. You can buy special covers on Amazon and other storefronts for this, but I usually just cut a small square from the sticky part of a Post-It. You can uncover and recover the camera more easily. If I don’t think I’ll ever use an embedded webcam in a laptop, I’ll use a bit of paper and tape. Note that this won’t solve the underlying cause of being spied on. Run a scan of your system with antivirus software, and also check for any unknown apps or browser extensions.

item.title: This free Windows app makes file conversion ridiculously easy
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Writing for a living means that I’m constantly converting text between Word documents and PDFs, or images into PNG or JPG files that I can use. Converting these files typically means either opening a separate app, uploading it to a website, or digging through a bunch of menus. File Converter cuts out all of that work by adding conversion tools right into the Windows context menu. Once you install File Converter, you’ll be able to right-click a supported file in File Explorer and choose File Converter . From there, pick the format you want to convert to and the app handles the rest. File Converter also allows you to process multiple conversions simultaneously if you have a bunch that you need to change. File Converter allows you to simply right-click on any file and convert it straight from the File Explorer menu. File Converter File Converter supports a wide range of formats. You can turn images into JPG, PNG, WebP, AVIF, and more, while audio files can be converted to MP3, WAV, FLAC, and so on. It also supports video formats like MP4, MKV, and WebM. If you want to convert Word, Excel, or PowerPoint files, however, you’ll need to have Microsoft Office installed and activated. I love tools like this that take a common annoyance completely out of the picture. If someone sends you a HEIC photo from their iPhone and you need it as a JPG on your desktop, or you want to shrink a video without opening a full video editor, it only takes a couple of clicks. You can also customize which conversion presets appear in the right-click menu and change settings for each one. Plus, File Converter is free, open source, has no ads, and says it doesn’t collect your data. Score one for privacy and convenience. Windows PCs with AMD Radeon GPUs—including the RX 6600, RX 7700 XT, RX 7800 XT, RX 7900 GRE, RX 7900 XTX, and RX 9070 XT—are still reporting driver timeouts, black screens, missing displays, and system crashes, even when not playing games. And issues with both File Explorer and File History , introduced with September’s Patch Tuesday updates, remain unresolved. You may find that new backups aren’t being made and previously made backups are no longer available, making your files unrecoverable. However, some problems have been fixed by an emergency update , including an issue affecting with Claude Cowork and Remote Desktop Services, as well as a fake Defender warning .

Working from home is the dream for many people. But despite being more comfortable than a traditional office, your home office may not be optimally suited for productivity. Our entire newsroom has had to adjust to remote work over the past few years—like most of the world—so we’ve spent a long time testing and reviewing hardware and optimizing our own workspaces. You don’t need to drop a ton of money on something expensive, either. A solid lightweight aluminum stand like the popular Lamicall Adjustable Laptop Stand will do just fine. It supports almost any laptop, from 10 inches up to 17.3 inches. It lets you adjust both tilt and height, and comes with ventilation holes to help dissipate laptop heat. It also comes with one of the best price-to-performance ratios of any SSD on the market. item.title: Want your laptop battery to last for years? Avoid these 9 mistakes
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
One of the most frustrating aspects of an aging laptop is how the battery life diminishes. Even super-long-lasting laptops eventually decay, and what once lasted a full day starts needing a charge before the work day ends. Before long, you’re using it plugged in all the time. But it doesn’t have to be this way! Modern laptops are designed to be efficient, long-lasting machines. If you treat them right and take good care of them, you can make sure the battery maintains its longevity for much longer—at least a few extra years. And if you don’t take good care of it? Well, expect the battery to lose capacity much sooner than you’d like. Here are some of the best habits you should practice if you want your laptop battery to truly last several years. (Not sure if your laptop battery is still good? Use this free tool to check it right now! ) Limit your battery’s max charge to 80% It might sound counterintuitive to reduce your overall battery capacity in order to get more out of it, but it’s true: keeping your battery at 100% for extended periods can accelerate wear and tear. That’s why you shouldn’t leave your laptop plugged in . Maxing out at around 80% reduces stress on the battery and slows its capacity loss over time. You’ll get less runtime per charge, but you’ll be able to enjoy that 80% capacity for much longer this way. (And if you won’t be using it for a long time, make sure it’s at 50% before storing it away.) Panos Sakalakis / Unsplash While Apple has a built-in feature on MacBooks for restricting max battery percentage, there’s no OS-specific solution for Windows 11. However, you might find such a setting in your laptop’s BIOS or your manufacturer’s specific utility app. The big-name brands—including Dell, Lenovo, HP, and Asus—usually offer a battery limiting feature. For older laptops, or ones that lack this feature for whatever reason, you’ll have to manually unplug your laptop from its charger whenever it reaches the desired charge capacity. Don’t let your battery hit 0% When a lithium-ion battery runs completely empty—and pretty much all laptops use lithium-ion batteries—the internal chemistry of the battery can become unstable. Long story short, draining a laptop battery to 0% can cause permanent wear and tear on the battery itself, impacting its ability to hold a charge and reducing its overall charge capacity. Make sure to recharge your laptop once it hits around 20% if you want to keep the battery healthy. At worst, don’t let it drop below 10%. Watch your laptop’s temperature Batteries have safe operating temperatures and you should do your best to keep them within that range. If you leave your laptop in the sun or in a hot car, you risk temperatures rising above that, which can accelerate wear and tear on the battery cells. In the worst extreme, it can even cause the battery to swell and risk catching fire. (At that point, you should immediately dispose of it because it’s a real hazard.) amt8u / Unsplash Don’t leave your laptop in your car or outside over night, either. Cold temperatures slow down the chemical reactions in lithium-ion batteries, potentially leading to reduced charge capacity. If you try to use the laptop while it’s super cold, that can also cause permanent damage to the battery cells. If your laptop ever gets particularly cold, let it warm up to room temperature before turning it on. Keeping the laptop at comfortable operating temperatures is a good idea in general, as an overheating laptop will reduce performance and system stability. Learn more about what to do if your laptop is overheating all the time . Keep it plugged in while gaming Modern laptops are designed to draw power from the outlet when plugged in, so if you’re going to be sitting at a desk for an extended time doing something intense—like gaming—then it makes sense to plug in. Thiago Trevisan / IDG By plugging in, you’ll get the full power of the laptop’s gaming ability (since they usually throttle, even if only partially, when running off battery power) and you’ll help preserve your battery’s lifespan by not putting it through constant drain-recharge cycles. In fact, if you’re gaming a lot, there’s a lot more you can do to keep your battery going strong for years. See our collection of tips for extending your gaming laptop’s battery life . Keep it clean and clear FeriDhaniHasri / Shutterstock If your laptop’s vents are dusty or dirty, its cooling can be affected. A hot laptop works harder to achieve the same performance, and the battery life will suffer in turn. Make sure to clean your laptop every few months to keep it in peak condition and prevent undue battery wear. Make sure you aren’t using it somewhere that’s blocking the vents, too. Soft blankets, sofas, cushions, and pillows are terrible surfaces for laptop use because they’re soft and comfort to the laptop, blocking vents and causing heat buildup. Hard surfaces allow for clear airflow and can make a big difference to laptop cooling, thus extending battery life. Optimize your power settings Windows 11 has a number of useful settings you can manage to improve battery life and help it last longer over the lifespan of your device. If you can get the battery to last longer on an individual charge, you’ll recharge it less often—and that’ll reduce wear on the battery over time. Jon Martindale / Foundry Navigate to Start > Settings > System > Power and battery > Screen and sleep to adjust how quickly your laptop goes into sleep mode and turns off its screen when on battery. If you leave your laptop idling a lot, cutting this down to just a few minutes can really help. If you want to extend your battery life temporarily, or once you pass a certain battery threshold, switch on Energy Saving Mode. Navigate to Start > Settings > System > Power and battery to turn it on or modify its settings. This’ll reduce performance, though, so only toggle this on if you really need it and don’t mind the sacrifice. You can also set it to “Balanced” or “Power Saver” power modes if you don’t need high-end gaming performance all the time. Navigate to Control Panel > System and Security > Power options and select the power plan that’s right for your needs. Tweak your screen Your laptop screen draws a lot of power, so adjusting its settings can impact your battery life. If you aren’t in a bright environment, lowering the screen brightness can go a long way to improving battery life. Your laptop should have keyboard shortcuts for this. Jon Martindale / Foundry You can also tweak the refresh rate. If you aren’t gaming, you don’t really need a 240Hz refresh rate (even if it does make your mouse pointer move more smoothly over the desktop and windows). Navigate to Settings > Display > Advanced Display to manually change your refresh rate to something lower. Alternatively, set it to Dynamic and your laptop will change the refresh rate as needed. Shut down background apps Unnecessary background apps will drain your battery life, and often you don’t need them running in the first place. Navigate to Start > Settings > System > Power and battery > Battery usage . Under Battery usage per app , you’ll be able to see which of your apps use the most power in the background. You can close them down, or stop them starting up with Windows entirely, to help extend your battery life and therefore boost your laptop’s overall battery longevity. Don’t forget to stay up-to-date Operating system and firmware updates aren’t going to magically make your laptop battery life longer, but Microsoft and laptop manufacturers do release efficiency and performance improvements sometimes. Making sure you’re fully up-to-date means your laptop is running as well as it can, and that’ll help your battery last longer. Further reading: Common mistakes that are killing your laptop

item.title: Claude Opus 5.5 promises to cut the chatter
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Better coding performance, improved safety and “alignment,” and greater value are among Anthropic’s selling points for its latest Claude Opus model. But for many Claude Opus users, one particular Opus 5.5 promise stands out: less chatter. Claude Opus 5.5 is the first new Claude model since Anthropic pledged to “pace” itself in the face of runaway AI development . In an eyebrow-raising coincidence, OpenAI (which has made similar promises to “pace” its AI work) announced its own new models — Sol and Luna variants of GPT-6 — barely two hours after Anthropic revealed the updated Opus. Now available across all Claude platforms, Claude Opus 5.5 has been trained to communicate “more naturally than prior models,” according to Anthropic’s press release , adding that “it puts the most important information up front, and its style makes it a better work partner over long sessions.” That’s no small thing. Claude Opus 5.5’s predecessor, Opus 5, is a notorious chatterbox, drafting meandering walls of text filled with asides, caveats, and — worst of all — “loose ends.” Opus 5’s loose ends, or “things I should flag,” or “items you should know about,” typically come after it has completed a task or delivered a finished product, compelling you to go back and deal with the dangling threads. Sometimes, Opus 5’s chronic need to leave extra follow-up items after a seemingly finished task felt like a ploy for more work, thus requiring users to spend more tokens. In a side-by-side comparison, Anthropic promises that Opus 5.5’s replies will get to the point more quickly, while also being “less likely to use jargon or idiosyncratic phrases.” In my limited testing of Opus 5.5 with Claude Code, the new model does seem far more direct, answering my questions succinctly without tacking on any loose ends or other random items to chase down. Aside from being far less loquacious, Opus 5.5 is the equal of Claude Fable 5.1 “on most work” while costing 40 percent less to operate than Opus 5, Anthropic says. Turing back to safety, Opus 5.5 is “much less likely than recent models to take hard-to-reverse actions or act outside the boundaries it’s been given,” Anthropic noted, adding that it “attempted to circumvent [containment] boundaries around 85 percent less often than Opus 5 or Claude Mythos 5.1.” (Personally, I’d prefer 100 percent less often, but I suppose that’s progress.) As part of its Opus 5.5 announcement, Anthropic said it’s boosting five-hour usage limits for Claude Pro, Max, and Team subscribers, while tossing in a gratis, one-time usage reset.

item.title: Google’s new Googlebook OS is basically Android for laptops
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
Not even a year ago, a rumor arose that Google was working on a new operating system for mobile platforms. Known as Aluminium OS , the OS would combine the best aspects of Android and ChromeOS, all while sidelining ChromeOS as Google’s OS of choice for laptops. Now, Aluminium OS is finally here… but under a completely different name. Because when Google officially unveiled its Googlebooks yesterday , it also marked the launch of Googlebook OS. While surprisingly uncreative in its name, it’s also admittedly a lot more straightforward than Aluminium OS. Developed specifically for its new laptops and largely based on Android 16 and Android 17, Googlebooks are clearly targeting Android users. Google’s first new OS in 15 years Unlike ChromeOS, Googlebook OS is designed to feel intuitive to anyone who has ever held an Android smartphone or tablet. It uses the new Material 3 Expressive Design, which has been in use since Android 16, and is therefore largely familiar. Under the hood, however, it also utilizes a Linux kernel, which is why Linux is supported natively . Google is promoting its new devices as a powerful alternative to Windows PCs and Macs. Googlebooks have access to numerous apps from the Google Play Store that are optimized for desktop use. These are by no means all the apps available on the Play Store, though, so the selection is still limited and there are some restrictions. Googlebooks are somewhat suitable for gaming too, partly thanks to controller support, but with a massive caveat: for demanding titles, users will need to stream via GeForce Now as the built-in hardware isn’t enough to run most triple-A games natively. Naturally, Googlebook OS relies heavily on AI. Google offers support for AI agents such as Claude CLI, and with Antigravity it also provides a built-in tool for developers who wish to program further AI support themselves. Google sees Googlebooks as more than just “AI PCs,” something for which Microsoft initially faced a lot of criticism with its Copilot+ PCs. Rather, a Googlebook can be used in close conjunction with an Android device by pairing the two. This allows not only files to be transferred seamlessly, but also apps—and that’s pretty handy if you find that you’re reaching the limits of your smaller device and/or need more power. 10 years of updates promised Another standout feature is that Google promises a full 10 years of updates for its Googlebooks. That’s an incredibly long time, considering how fast-moving software and hardware have become. During that period, a new update is expected to release every three months. However, even these new devices aren’t immune to rising hardware prices. The more affordable Googlebooks from Dell and HP start at $899 while models from other manufacturers can reach $1,299 or higher.

item.title: Lock down your Windows 11 taskbar so no one else can change it
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
The Windows taskbar is a pretty nifty thing, offering a wide range of customization options. You can change its position, size, the buttons displayed, the pinned programs, the appearance of the search box, and much more. However, if multiple people use the computer, they might adjust those settings to suit their personal preferences. This means the administrator will have to manually restore the taskbar to its default state. That said, you can make some of those settings inaccessible. There are two ways to do this: you can freeze the current settings or prevent users from making changes to the taskbar. Both can be done using the Registry or Group Policy. The Group Policy Editor is available in Windows Professional, as well as the Education and Business editions. To completely prevent changes to the taskbar using the Registry, type regedit into the search box and click on Registry Editor. Now, navigate to this folder: HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Policies\Explorer . Select Explorer. Right-click in the right-hand pane and choose New → DWORD (32-bit) Value. Name the new value TaskbarLockAll. Right-click on it, select Modify, enter 1 as the value, and confirm by clicking OK. Foundry Now go to Personalization → Taskbar in Windows Settings. Some options (like the option to automatically hide the taskbar) will be greyed out. You’ll find the same setting in the Group Policy Editor. Type gpedit into the search box and open the editor. Go to User Configuration → Administrative Templates → Start Menu and Taskbar, and double-click Lock all Taskbar Settings. Select Enabled and confirm by clicking OK. To prevent standard users from making changes to the taskbar, open the Registry and navigate (again) to the folder HKEY_CURRENT_USER\Software\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\Explorer . Right-click in the right-hand pane and select New → DWORD (32-bit) Value. Name the new entry NoSetTaskbar and set the value to 1. In the Group Policy Editor, you’ll find the same setting under User Configuration → Administrative Templates → Start Menu and Taskbar. Double-click on Prevent Changes to the Taskbar and Start Menu Settings and set the status to Enabled.

item.title: How to make CC emails stand out in Outlook
item.description:
Source: PCWorld Pre-analysis score: 0.84
You probably get plenty of emails that are there to just keep you informed. You’re CC’d on the message, but you’re not actually expected to respond. If you want to make these emails easier to spot, you can set Outlook to highlight them in a different color. Here’s how to do it: If you’re using the classic version of Outlook, go to View > View Options > Conditional Formatting. Next, click Add and enter a name such as CC Emails. Click on Font, set the color (something bright and distinctive), and close the window by confirming with OK. In the Messages tab, click on Condition. Tick the box next to In Which I and, in the menu to the right, select the option I am listed with other recipients on the CC line. Close the windows by clicking OK. The new version of Outlook supports this highlighting feature, too. First, go to View > View Settings and then select Mail on the left-hand side. In the second column, select Conditional Formatting and click Add Rule in the right-hand pane. Enter CC email as the name for the new rule and, in the Condition menu, select the option I am listed in the CC field. Nest, click on Select Color and pick your favorite hue. Confirm by clicking OK and Save, then close the window.
